The Emperor of Japan who reigned during World I was **Emperor Taishō** (Yoshihito Shinnō).  
His **official mother** was **Empress Dowager Shōken** (born Lady Ichijō Haruko).  

Shōken was the consort of Emperor Meiji and, after his death in 1912, was granted the title of Empress Dowager. She was considered the legal mother of her adopted son, Prince Yoshihito, who became Emperor Taishō. (His biological mother was Lady Yanagihara Naruko, a concubine of Emperor Meiji.)

**Emperor Taishō**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Taish%C5%8D#cite_note-1) (31 August 1879–25 December 1926), personal name (_imina_) **Yoshihito**, was Emperor of Japan from 29 July 1912 until his death in 1926. His reign was marked by a domestic political shift toward liberal democracy, called Taishō Democracy. He oversaw Japan's participation in World War I on the side of the Allies, the Spanish flu epidemic, and the Great Kantō Earthquake of 1923. His poor health limited his public duties and contributed to his death at age 47.
Born to Emperor Meiji and his concubine Yanagiwara Naruko, Yoshihito was proclaimed crown prince and heir apparent in 1888, his two older siblings having died in infancy. He suffered various health problems as a child, including meningitis soon after his birth. In 1900, he married Sadako Kujō, a member of the Kujō family of the Fujiwara clan; the couple had four sons. In 1912, Yoshihito became emperor upon the death of his father, but as he suffered from neurological issues for much of his life, he played only a limited role in politics and undertook no official duties from 1919. His declining health led to the appointment of his eldest son, Crown Prince Hirohito, as regent in 1921, and Hirohito succeeded him as emperor when he died aged 47 at Hayama Imperial Villa in Kanagawa Prefecture.

Prince Yoshihito was born at the Tōgū Palace in Akasaka, Tokyo to Emperor Meiji and Yanagiwara Naruko, a concubine with the official title of _gon-no-tenji_ (imperial concubine). As was common practice at the time, Emperor Meiji's consort, Empress Shōken, was officially regarded as his mother. He received the personal name of Yoshihito Shinnō and the title _Haru-no-miya_ from the Emperor on 6 September 1879. His two older siblings had died in infancy, and he too, was born sickly.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Taish%C5%8D#cite_note-2)
Prince Yoshihito contracted cerebral meningitis within three weeks of his birth.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Taish%C5%8D#cite_note-Bix,_Page_22-3)
As was the practice at the time, Prince Yoshihito was entrusted to the care of his great-grandfather, Marquess Nakayama Tadayasu, in whose house he lived from infancy until the age of seven. Prince Nakayama had also raised Taishō's father, the Emperor Meiji, as a child.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Taish%C5%8D#cite_note-4)
From March 1885, Prince Yoshihito moved to the Aoyama Detached Palace, where he was tutored in the mornings on reading, writing, arithmetic, and morals, and in the afternoons on sports, but progress was slow due to his poor health and frequent fevers.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Taish%C5%8D#cite_note-Keene,_page_397-398-5) From 1886, he was taught together with 15–20 selected classmates from the _ōke_ and higher ranking _kazoku_ peerage at a special school, the _Gogakumonsho_, within the Aoyama Palace.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Taish%C5%8D#cite_note-Keene,_page_397-398-5)

Yoshihito was officially declared heir on 31 August 1887, and had his formal investiture as crown prince on 3 November 1888. While crown prince, he was often referred to simply as **Tōgu** (東宮) ('Eastern Palace', a metonymy for heir to the throne, which originated from China'sHan dynasty).
Crown Prince Tōgu with his father and stepmother strolling in Asukayama Park accompanied by ladies of the court. Colour woodblock print by Yōshū Chikanobu, 1890

### Education and training
[edit]
When Yoshihito became of the age to enter elementary school in 1886, due to his health problems, Takehiko Yumoto was appointed as the special education officer to educate him within the Tōgū Palace.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Taish%C5%8D#cite_note-6) For these health reasons, he spent much of his youth at the Imperial villas at Hayama and Numazu, both of which are located by the sea. Although the prince showed skill in some areas, such as horse riding, he proved to be poor in areas requiring higher-level thought._[citation needed_] He was finally withdrawn from Gakushuin before finishing the middle school course in 1894. However, he did appear to have an aptitude for languages and continued to receive extensive tutoring in French, Chinese, and history from private tutors at the Akasaka Palace;_[citation needed_] Emperor Meiji gave Prince Takehito responsibility for taking care of Prince Yoshihito, and the two princes became friends.
From 1898, largely at the insistence of Itō Hirobumi, the Prince began to attend sessions of the House of Peers of the Diet of Japan as a way of learning about the political and military concerns of the country. In the same year, he gave his first official receptions to foreign diplomats, with whom he was able to shake hands and converse graciously.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Taish%C5%8D#cite_note-7) His infatuation with western culture and tendency to sprinkle French words into his conversations was a source of irritation for Emperor Meiji.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Taish%C5%8D#cite_note-8)
In October 1898, the Prince also traveled from the Numazu Imperial Villa to Kobe, Hiroshima, and Etajima, visiting sites connected with the Imperial Japanese Navy. He made another tour in 1899 to Kyūshū, visiting government offices, schools and factories (such as Yawata Iron and Steel in Fukuoka and the Mitsubishi shipyards in Nagasaki).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Taish%C5%8D#cite_note-9)

From this point onward, the Empress and her entourage wore only Western-style clothes in public. In January 1887 Empress Haruko herself issued a memorandum on the subject, stating traditional Japanese dress was not only unsuited to modern life, but Western-style dress was closer than the kimono to the clothes worn by ancient Japanese women.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empress_Sh%C5%8Dken#cite_note-6)
In the diplomatic field, Empress Haruko hosted the wife of former United States PresidentUlysses S. Grant during his visit to Japan. She was also present for her husband's meetings with Hawaiian KingKalākaua in 1881. Later that same year, she helped host the visit of the sons of future British KingEdward VII: Princes Albert Victor and George (later George V), who presented her with a pair of pet wallabies from Australia.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empress_Sh%C5%8Dken#cite_note-7)
The Emperor and the Empress ride a horse-drawn carriage to attend the constitutional celebration on 11 February 1889.
On 26 November 1886, Empress Haruko accompanied her husband to Yokosuka, Kanagawa to observe the new Imperial Japanese Navycruisers_Naniwa_ and _Takachiho_ firing torpedoes and performing other maneuvers. From 1887, the Empress was often at the Emperor's side in official visits to army maneuvers.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empress_Sh%C5%8Dken#cite_note-8) When Emperor Meiji fell ill in 1888, Empress Haruko took his place in welcoming envoys from Siam, launching warships, and visiting Tokyo Imperial University.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empress_Sh%C5%8Dken#cite_note-9) In 1889, Empress Haruko accompanied Emperor Meiji on an official visit to Nagoya and the former imperial capital of Kyoto. While he continued on to inspect naval bases at Kure and Sasebo, she visited Nara to worship at the principal Shinto shrines.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empress_Sh%C5%8Dken#cite_note-10)

Known throughout her tenure for supporting charity work and women's education during the First Sino-Japanese War (1894–95), Empress Haruko worked for the establishment of the Japanese Red Cross Society. She participated in the Society’s administration, especially in peacetime activities wherein she created a money fund for the International Red Cross. Renamed "The Empress Shōken Fund", it is presently used for international welfare activities. After Emperor Meiji moved his military headquarters from Tokyo to Hiroshima to be closer to the lines of communications with his troops, Empress Haruko joined him in March 1895. While in Hiroshima, she insisted on visiting hospitals full of wounded soldiers every other day of her stay.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empress_Sh%C5%8Dken#cite_note-11)
After Emperor Meiji's death in 1912, Empress Haruko was granted the title Empress Dowager (皇太后, _Kōtaigō_) by her adoptive son, Emperor Taishō. She died in 1914 at the Imperial Villa in Numazu, Shizuoka and was buried in the East Mound of the _Fushimi Momoyama Ryo_ in Fushimi, Kyoto, next to her husband. The Meiji Shrine in Tokyo was dedicated to her and her late husband.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empress_Sh%C5%8Dken#cite_note-12) On 9 May 1914, she received the posthumous name "Empress Dowager Shōken" (昭憲皇太后, _Shōken Kōtaigō_).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empress_Sh%C5%8Dken#cite_note-IHMA9th1914-1) Her railway-carriage can be seen today in the Meiji Mura Museum, in Inuyama, Aichi prefecture.

Empress Dowager Shōken (しょうけんこうたいごう, May 9, 1849 – April 9, 1914), formerly known as Ichijō Haruko, was the Empress consort of Emperor Meiji of Japan and the legal mother of Emperor Taishō. Born into a court noble family, she experienced enhanced intellectual development in her childhood due to a special diet, earning her the title "Tengu daughter" from Emperor Meiji. She married Emperor Meiji in 1867.
She spearheaded the establishment of Tokyo Women's Normal School, promoting the development of Japan's new-style women's education system. From 1887, she sponsored the development of the Japanese Red Cross Society; the "Empress Shōken Fund" established with her donations was adopted by the International Red Cross. In the political sphere, she assisted Emperor Meiji indirectly, mediating conflicts between the Emperor and Itō Hirobumi and conducting social activities among noble ladies through her court ladies. In her lifetime, she composed 30,000 waka poems and authored The Collected Poems of Empress Dowager Shōken.

Empress Dowager Shōken (しょうけんこうたいごう), formerly known as Ichijō Haruko (いちじょう はるこ), lived from Kaei 2, 4th month, 17th day (May 9, 1849) to Taishō 3 (April 11, 1914). She was the wife of Emperor Meiji. She was the daughter of Ichijō Tadaka, the Left Minister of the First Rank. This lady, along with the Kujō family, was a core member of the Kōbu gattai faction, was implicated in the Ansei Purge, and ultimately retired from public life under censure from the Sonnō jōi faction. Ichijō Tadaka's political abilities were not outstanding; among the court nobles of the Bakumatsu period, only Sanjō Sanetomi and Iwakura Tomomi could be considered significant figures. However, Ichijō Tadaka had his own exceptional talent: he knew how to raise daughters. In addition to marrying his biological daughter Haruko to the future Emperor Meiji, he also strongly advocated for his adopted daughter, Ichijō Mikako, to marry Tokugawa Yoshinobu, making her the last Official wife of the Tokugawa shogun of the Tokugawa family.
Empress Shōken was not originally named Ichijō Haruko. In her childhood, her name was Katsuko. In June 1858, Ichijō Tadaka, caught in the vortex of the Ansei Purge, gave his daughter the name "Suehime" (Princess Sue), somewhat to ward off bad luck. Perhaps the prayers were effective, as Ichijō ultimately received only a light punishment of ten days of caution and self-reflection, far milder than the forced resignation and seclusion imposed on others like Takatsukasa.

At this time, Ichijō Haruko suffered from a common ailment among children of court noble families: malnutrition. The food of court nobles at the time was too refined, leading to a severe deficiency in protein intake. To nurse the sickly and weak Haruko back to health, the Ichijō family often had her eat fish and eggs. Unexpectedly, this led to Haruko's intellectual development far surpassing that of her peers from other court noble families. She possessed a remarkable memory, was proficient in all the arts of music, chess, calligraphy, and painting, and excelled in tea ceremony, flower arrangement, koto playing, and waka poetry. Her cleverness and quick wit led Emperor Meiji to admiringly call Haruko "Tengu daughter".
Between Teacher and Student
On January 30, 1867, Emperor Kōmei died suddenly. On February 14, Emperor Meiji, just 14 years old, ascended the throne. The court nobles hurriedly made arrangements to find a wife for the new emperor. At that time, rumors that Emperor Kōmei had been assassinated by the Tōbaku faction were rampant, causing panic among the nobles of the Kōbu gattai faction. Therefore, Empress Dowager Eishō, who also hailed from the Kōbu gattai faction, strongly advocated that her adopted son marry a wife from a Kōbu gattai family. The Ichijō family was considered a suitable match. On July 29, Ichijō Haruko was designated as the new emperor's empress. Subsequently, Empress Ichijō changed her childhood name Katsuko to Haruko.

The Japanese Imperial Family placed great importance on the education of the empress. On September 6, 1867, the Imperial Household selected the renowned female Confucian scholar Wakae Kaoruko to serve as Haruko's tutor. Speaking of Wakae Kaoruko, she was quite an extraordinary woman. Because she was considered ugly since childhood, Kaoruko devoted herself to scholarly pursuits. By the age of fifteen or sixteen, she had already studied the classics, histories, and works of various philosophers. Not only was she proficient in Chinese studies, but she was also a staunch member of the Sonnō jōi faction. Wakae Kaoruko's education of Ichijō Haruko was extremely strict. According to Kaoruko's recollections, Haruko, who was in her early teens and mischievous, was often scolded to tears by her stern female tutor. However, the relationship between teacher and student was very good. Haruko's political ideology did not follow her father's but instead aligned with her tutor's, making her a staunch supporter of Sonnō (Revere the Emperor). However, precisely because Kaoruko's influence over the empress was so significant, after the Meiji Restoration, the Kaikoku faction, fearing the Sonnō jōi faction might exploit Kaoruko and the empress, seized the opportunity in 1869 when Kaoruko expressed sympathy for the rōnin who assassinated Yokoi Shōnan to expel Kaoruko from the court.

The Kaikoku faction's concerns were not without reason. The politics of the "Official wife of the Tokugawa shogun" (the shogun's wife) in Japan had a history almost as long as the cloistered government system. Both the Fujiwara and Toyotomi families had numerous politically powerful women who influenced state affairs under titles like "Kitamandokoro" and "Ōmandokoro." After the Meiji Restoration, with the introduction of Western feminism, the influence of the emperor's empress became even stronger than that of the Tokugawa Midaidokoro. However, at this time, Haruko lost the position of Chūgūshoku, which had been the office of the Japanese emperor's principal wife since the Middle Ages. In 1870, as part of court reforms, the Chūgūshoku was replaced by the Kōgōgūshoku, making Haruko Japan's last Chūgū and first Kōgōgū. Despite the name change, Haruko's influence over Emperor Meiji remained constant. Emperor Meiji was born in November 1852, while Haruko was born in May 1849; she was more than three years older than her husband. According to imperial tradition, relationships where the woman was more than three years older were to be avoided. Therefore, the Imperial Household publicly announced Haruko's birth year as 1850.
New-Style Women's Education
Empress Dowager Shōken
The Kaikoku faction's brainwashing-style Westernization education for the Empress was quite successful. Although Haruko received a Confucian education from a young age, after the opening of the country, she demonstrated an extremely progressive attitude, displaying the demeanor of a Western-style women's activist. The new-style education system for the Japanese imperial family was largely established under Haruko's leadership. She contributed significantly to the establishment of Japan's Red Cross, or the military medical relief system. Most importantly, Empress Dowager Shōken established a model for future female members of the imperial family: that of a virtuous helpmate who governs through inaction under a constitutional system.

Furthermore, Shōken consistently paid attention to maintaining the image of her husband, Emperor Meiji, especially when the Emperor put on airs. For instance, also in 1884, Yoshii Tomozane, who had just been appointed as the Vice-Minister of the Imperial Household and was the former president of the Nippon Tetsudōsha (Japan Railway Company), respectfully invited the Emperor and Empress to attend the opening ceremony of the Ueno to Takasaki railway. Yoshii was a rather well-known proponent of enlightenment (kaikaha) and was placed near Emperor Meiji by Itō and other Meiji Restoration leaders as "sand" to dilute the conservative atmosphere surrounding the Emperor. Naturally, Emperor Meiji was very dissatisfied with this Vice-Minister of the Imperial Household who had been forced upon him and seized the opportunity to snub him. On the day of the opening ceremony, the Emperor publicly complained about the rain in a huff and left midway. Yoshii, left stranded at the scene, was extremely embarrassed. Unexpectedly, the Emperor's wife then performed with exceptional magnanimity and grace. She not only remained present throughout the entire ceremony but also continuously smiled and offered congratulations to Yoshii. The deeply moved old Yoshii later wrote to his friends extensively praising "Long live the Empress!"
Empress Shōken was devoted to the affairs of the Japanese Red Cross Society, yet there are no records of this Empress expressing anti-war sentiments. On the contrary, as a model for militaristic women of the time, she made every effort to boost morale and raise military funds during both the First China’s War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and the Russo-Japanese War. A well-known anecdote recounts that on the eve of the Russo-Japanese War, February 7, 1904, while resting at the Hayama Imperial Villa, Empress Shōken dreamed of a 37 or 38-year-old warrior dressed in white who pledged to the Empress Dowager that he would protect the Japanese Combined Fleet. The startled Empress Dowager described the vision to her attendants. The palace official Kagawa Keizō asserted that this was the spirit of Sakamoto Ryōma manifesting itself. He quickly seized upon this supernatural event for extensive propaganda, which momentarily boosted public morale and fighting spirit. From then on, Sakamoto Ryōma was formally enshrined as a guardian deity of the
Japanese Navy
.

Wives' Politics
In this subtle and imperceptible manner, Empress Haruko assisted Emperor Meiji. Furthermore, for other political matters where it was inconvenient for her to appear personally, such as courting the wives of the major figures of the Restoration to engage in "wives' politics," Haruko relied on the court lady Shimoda Utako to carry out these tasks.
One might ask why Her Majesty the Empress could not handle the "wives' politics" herself. The main reason was the problematic backgrounds of the wives of the Restoration leaders. While some of the Restoration activists, like Saigō Takamori, were high-ranking samurai from powerful anti-shogunate domains, the vast majority were low-ranking samurai or even ruffians and rascals. These men were frequent patrons of the pleasure quarters, and naturally, their wives were often chosen from among the courtesans.
Take the famous Katsura Kogorō, for example. His wife, Kido Matsuko, one of the "Three Great Nobles of the Restoration," was a renowned geisha known by the professional name "Ikumatsu" before their marriage. Many other wives of the newly ennobled kazoku (peers) also came from the pleasure quarters. Consequently, the established aristocracy, especially the imperial family, disdained associating with these women of humble origin. However, Haruko's cleverness lay in finding a method that neither offended the conservative traditionalists nor failed to leverage the influence of these wives. This was achieved by requesting the retired court lady Shimoda Utako to establish the "Tōyō Juku," a school specifically to educate the new noblewomen who, despite their lowly origins, were exceptionally intelligent. Many graduates of the "Tōyō Juku" later became strong supporters of modern education.

Additionally, Empress Haruko also paid attention to helping the Emperor win over the disaffected remnants of the old order. During the Bakumatsu period and the early Meiji era, amidst successive political upheavals and bloody conflicts, the Tokugawa family fell, the pro-shogunate domains collapsed, and soon even the powerful anti-shogunate domains were dismantled through the return of the land and people registers. This is to say nothing of the tens of thousands who fell in the Boshin War, the Tōhoku War, and the Satsuma Rebellion, nor the large numbers of shizoku (former samurai) who were impoverished and bankrupted by the stipend reforms. The intense social transformation caused severe turmoil and opposition, leading to constant assassinations and conspiracies throughout the Bakumatsu and early Restoration period.
Although the Meiji government ultimately emerged victorious, it was widely understood that Japanese society would struggle to move forward unburdened unless the resentment of the defeated could be quickly assuaged. Against this backdrop, Kagawa Keizō, the Chief Chamberlain of the Empress's Household, stepped forward. He began touring various regions to conduct bereaved family consolation work, rehabilitating and restoring the honor of those who had been defeated in the past. Empress Haruko wisely remained behind the scenes, continuously using her influence to quietly remove obstacles one by one in this nationwide effort to heal wounds.
Anecdotes
Emperor Meiji playfully called his wife "
Tengu
daughter," which was closely related to Haruko's prominent, upturned nose. In Japan at that time, it was considered desirable for women to have high, straight noses with nostrils facing forward, to the extent that some even underwent procedures to achieve this. Additionally, Empress Haruko enjoyed smoking, and every time she blew smoke rings from her nose, it would make Emperor Meiji laugh heartily. This was because, in Japanese folklore, a Tengu is depicted with a long, chimney-like nose and is also said to be fond of smoking. However, since Emperor Meiji himself did not smoke, Empress Haruko, considering that the emperor's nickname "Tengu daughter" for her might also carry a hint of teasing, subsequently became mindful and never smoked in her husband's presence again.

Haruko was also a highly accomplished female artist. Throughout her life, she composed thirty thousand waka poems. After her passing, a collection titled The Collected Poems of Empress Dowager Shōken was published. In 1876, she personally composed and bestowed a school song upon the Tokyo Women's Normal School. Furthermore, the school song currently used by Gakushūin Women's Junior and Senior High School, which evolved from the Peeresses' School, was also composed by Haruko. She also paid great attention to encouraging the Japanese sericulture industry, an initiative that had been promoted since the time of the previous Empress Dowager Eishō, often bestowing monetary rewards and gifts. Other endeavors, such as Japan's earliest systems for orphan adoption and education, also have significant connections to Empress Haruko.
Many aspects of the attire and demeanor of the Japanese Imperial Family and even Japanese women today trace their origins to Empress Dowager Shōken. However, at that time, under Haruko's leadership, the imperial family took the lead in adopting Western clothing. Even Emperor Meiji was persuaded by his wife on this matter, which frequently led to heated arguments between conservative elders like Motoda and the empress's lady-in-waiting, Shimoda Utako. Even in her old age, Haruko maintained her wisdom. It is said that just two days before her death, she expelled corrupt individuals engaged in embezzlement and bribery from the imperial court. It is no wonder that upon the death of this Eastern empress, even the British newspaper The Times published a dedicated article in her memory.

Empress Dowager Shōken (しょうけんこうたいごう, May 9, 1849 – April 9, 1914), formerly known as Ichijō Haruko, was the Empress consort of Emperor Meiji of Japan and the legal mother of Emperor Taishō. Born into a court noble family, she experienced enhanced intellectual development in her childhood due to a special diet, earning her the title "Tengu daughter" from Emperor Meiji. She married Emperor Meiji in 1867.
She spearheaded the establishment of Tokyo Women's Normal School, promoting the development of Japan's new-style women's education system. From 1887, she sponsored the development of the Japanese Red Cross Society; the "Empress Shōken Fund" established with her donations was adopted by the International Red Cross. In the political sphere, she assisted Emperor Meiji indirectly, mediating conflicts between the Emperor and Itō Hirobumi and conducting social activities among noble ladies through her court ladies. In her lifetime, she composed 30,000 waka poems and authored The Collected Poems of Empress Dowager Shōken.

Empress Dowager Shōken (しょうけんこうたいごう), formerly known as Ichijō Haruko (いちじょう はるこ), lived from Kaei 2, 4th month, 17th day (May 9, 1849) to Taishō 3 (April 11, 1914). She was the wife of Emperor Meiji. She was the daughter of Ichijō Tadaka, the Left Minister of the First Rank. This lady, along with the Kujō family, was a core member of the Kōbu gattai faction, was implicated in the Ansei Purge, and ultimately retired from public life under censure from the Sonnō jōi faction. Ichijō Tadaka's political abilities were not outstanding; among the court nobles of the Bakumatsu period, only Sanjō Sanetomi and Iwakura Tomomi could be considered significant figures. However, Ichijō Tadaka had his own exceptional talent: he knew how to raise daughters. In addition to marrying his biological daughter Haruko to the future Emperor Meiji, he also strongly advocated for his adopted daughter, Ichijō Mikako, to marry Tokugawa Yoshinobu, making her the last Official wife of the Tokugawa shogun of the Tokugawa family.
Empress Shōken was not originally named Ichijō Haruko. In her childhood, her name was Katsuko. In June 1858, Ichijō Tadaka, caught in the vortex of the Ansei Purge, gave his daughter the name "Suehime" (Princess Sue), somewhat to ward off bad luck. Perhaps the prayers were effective, as Ichijō ultimately received only a light punishment of ten days of caution and self-reflection, far milder than the forced resignation and seclusion imposed on others like Takatsukasa.
texts.2:
At this time, Ichijō Haruko suffered from a common ailment among children of court noble families: malnutrition. The food of court nobles at the time was too refined, leading to a severe deficiency in protein intake. To nurse the sickly and weak Haruko back to health, the Ichijō family often had her eat fish and eggs. Unexpectedly, this led to Haruko's intellectual development far surpassing that of her peers from other court noble families. She possessed a remarkable memory, was proficient in all the arts of music, chess, calligraphy, and painting, and excelled in tea ceremony, flower arrangement, koto playing, and waka poetry. Her cleverness and quick wit led Emperor Meiji to admiringly call Haruko "Tengu daughter".
Between Teacher and Student
On January 30, 1867, Emperor Kōmei died suddenly. On February 14, Emperor Meiji, just 14 years old, ascended the throne. The court nobles hurriedly made arrangements to find a wife for the new emperor. At that time, rumors that Emperor Kōmei had been assassinated by the Tōbaku faction were rampant, causing panic among the nobles of the Kōbu gattai faction. Therefore, Empress Dowager Eishō, who also hailed from the Kōbu gattai faction, strongly advocated that her adopted son marry a wife from a Kōbu gattai family. The Ichijō family was considered a suitable match. On July 29, Ichijō Haruko was designated as the new emperor's empress. Subsequently, Empress Ichijō changed her childhood name Katsuko to Haruko.
texts.3: The Japanese Imperial Family placed great importance on the education of the empress. On September 6, 1867, the Imperial Household selected the renowned female Confucian scholar Wakae Kaoruko to serve as Haruko's tutor. Speaking of Wakae Kaoruko, she was quite an extraordinary woman. Because she was considered ugly since childhood, Kaoruko devoted herself to scholarly pursuits. By the age of fifteen or sixteen, she had already studied the classics, histories, and works of various philosophers. Not only was she proficient in Chinese studies, but she was also a staunch member of the Sonnō jōi faction. Wakae Kaoruko's education of Ichijō Haruko was extremely strict. According to Kaoruko's recollections, Haruko, who was in her early teens and mischievous, was often scolded to tears by her stern female tutor. However, the relationship between teacher and student was very good. Haruko's political ideology did not follow her father's but instead aligned with her tutor's, making her a staunch supporter of Sonnō (Revere the Emperor). However, precisely because Kaoruko's influence over the empress was so significant, after the Meiji Restoration, the Kaikoku faction, fearing the Sonnō jōi faction might exploit Kaoruko and the empress, seized the opportunity in 1869 when Kaoruko expressed sympathy for the rōnin who assassinated Yokoi Shōnan to expel Kaoruko from the court.
texts.4:
The Kaikoku faction's concerns were not without reason. The politics of the "Official wife of the Tokugawa shogun" (the shogun's wife) in Japan had a history almost as long as the cloistered government system. Both the Fujiwara and Toyotomi families had numerous politically powerful women who influenced state affairs under titles like "Kitamandokoro" and "Ōmandokoro." After the Meiji Restoration, with the introduction of Western feminism, the influence of the emperor's empress became even stronger than that of the Tokugawa Midaidokoro. However, at this time, Haruko lost the position of Chūgūshoku, which had been the office of the Japanese emperor's principal wife since the Middle Ages. In 1870, as part of court reforms, the Chūgūshoku was replaced by the Kōgōgūshoku, making Haruko Japan's last Chūgū and first Kōgōgū. Despite the name change, Haruko's influence over Emperor Meiji remained constant. Emperor Meiji was born in November 1852, while Haruko was born in May 1849; she was more than three years older than her husband. According to imperial tradition, relationships where the woman was more than three years older were to be avoided. Therefore, the Imperial Household publicly announced Haruko's birth year as 1850.
New-Style Women's Education
Empress Dowager Shōken
The Kaikoku faction's brainwashing-style Westernization education for the Empress was quite successful. Although Haruko received a Confucian education from a young age, after the opening of the country, she demonstrated an extremely progressive attitude, displaying the demeanor of a Western-style women's activist. The new-style education system for the Japanese imperial family was largely established under Haruko's leadership. She contributed significantly to the establishment of Japan's Red Cross, or the military medical relief system. Most importantly, Empress Dowager Shōken established a model for future female members of the imperial family: that of a virtuous helpmate who governs through inaction under a constitutional system.
texts.10:
Furthermore, Shōken consistently paid attention to maintaining the image of her husband, Emperor Meiji, especially when the Emperor put on airs. For instance, also in 1884, Yoshii Tomozane, who had just been appointed as the Vice-Minister of the Imperial Household and was the former president of the Nippon Tetsudōsha (Japan Railway Company), respectfully invited the Emperor and Empress to attend the opening ceremony of the Ueno to Takasaki railway. Yoshii was a rather well-known proponent of enlightenment (kaikaha) and was placed near Emperor Meiji by Itō and other Meiji Restoration leaders as "sand" to dilute the conservative atmosphere surrounding the Emperor. Naturally, Emperor Meiji was very dissatisfied with this Vice-Minister of the Imperial Household who had been forced upon him and seized the opportunity to snub him. On the day of the opening ceremony, the Emperor publicly complained about the rain in a huff and left midway. Yoshii, left stranded at the scene, was extremely embarrassed. Unexpectedly, the Emperor's wife then performed with exceptional magnanimity and grace. She not only remained present throughout the entire ceremony but also continuously smiled and offered congratulations to Yoshii. The deeply moved old Yoshii later wrote to his friends extensively praising "Long live the Empress!"
Empress Shōken was devoted to the affairs of the Japanese Red Cross Society, yet there are no records of this Empress expressing anti-war sentiments. On the contrary, as a model for militaristic women of the time, she made every effort to boost morale and raise military funds during both the First China’s War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and the Russo-Japanese War. A well-known anecdote recounts that on the eve of the Russo-Japanese War, February 7, 1904, while resting at the Hayama Imperial Villa, Empress Shōken dreamed of a 37 or 38-year-old warrior dressed in white who pledged to the Empress Dowager that he would protect the Japanese Combined Fleet. The startled Empress Dowager described the vision to her attendants. The palace official Kagawa Keizō asserted that this was the spirit of Sakamoto Ryōma manifesting itself. He quickly seized upon this supernatural event for extensive propaganda, which momentarily boosted public morale and fighting spirit. From then on, Sakamoto Ryōma was formally enshrined as a guardian deity of the
Japanese Navy
.

texts.1:
**Emperor Taishō**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Taish%C5%8D#cite_note-1) (31 August 1879–25 December 1926), personal name (_imina_) **Yoshihito**, was Emperor of Japan from 29 July 1912 until his death in 1926. His reign was marked by a domestic political shift toward liberal democracy, called Taishō Democracy. He oversaw Japan's participation in World War I on the side of the Allies, the Spanish flu epidemic, and the Great Kantō Earthquake of 1923. His poor health limited his public duties and contributed to his death at age 47.
Born to Emperor Meiji and his concubine Yanagiwara Naruko, Yoshihito was proclaimed crown prince and heir apparent in 1888, his two older siblings having died in infancy. He suffered various health problems as a child, including meningitis soon after his birth. In 1900, he married Sadako Kujō, a member of the Kujō family of the Fujiwara clan; the couple had four sons. In 1912, Yoshihito became emperor upon the death of his father, but as he suffered from neurological issues for much of his life, he played only a limited role in politics and undertook no official duties from 1919. His declining health led to the appointment of his eldest son, Crown Prince Hirohito, as regent in 1921, and Hirohito succeeded him as emperor when he died aged 47 at Hayama Imperial Villa in Kanagawa Prefecture.
texts.2:
Prince Yoshihito was born at the Tōgū Palace in Akasaka, Tokyo to Emperor Meiji and Yanagiwara Naruko, a concubine with the official title of _gon-no-tenji_ (imperial concubine). As was common practice at the time, Emperor Meiji's consort, Empress Shōken, was officially regarded as his mother. He received the personal name of Yoshihito Shinnō and the title _Haru-no-miya_ from the Emperor on 6 September 1879. His two older siblings had died in infancy, and he too, was born sickly.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Taish%C5%8D#cite_note-2)
Prince Yoshihito contracted cerebral meningitis within three weeks of his birth.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Taish%C5%8D#cite_note-Bix,_Page_22-3)
As was the practice at the time, Prince Yoshihito was entrusted to the care of his great-grandfather, Marquess Nakayama Tadayasu, in whose house he lived from infancy until the age of seven. Prince Nakayama had also raised Taishō's father, the Emperor Meiji, as a child.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Taish%C5%8D#cite_note-4)
From March 1885, Prince Yoshihito moved to the Aoyama Detached Palace, where he was tutored in the mornings on reading, writing, arithmetic, and morals, and in the afternoons on sports, but progress was slow due to his poor health and frequent fevers.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Taish%C5%8D#cite_note-Keene,_page_397-398-5) From 1886, he was taught together with 15–20 selected classmates from the _ōke_ and higher ranking _kazoku_ peerage at a special school, the _Gogakumonsho_, within the Aoyama Palace.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Taish%C5%8D#cite_note-Keene,_page_397-398-5)
texts.3:
Yoshihito was officially declared heir on 31 August 1887, and had his formal investiture as crown prince on 3 November 1888. While crown prince, he was often referred to simply as **Tōgu** (東宮) ('Eastern Palace', a metonymy for heir to the throne, which originated from China'sHan dynasty).
Crown Prince Tōgu with his father and stepmother strolling in Asukayama Park accompanied by ladies of the court. Colour woodblock print by Yōshū Chikanobu, 1890
texts.4:
### Education and training
[edit]
When Yoshihito became of the age to enter elementary school in 1886, due to his health problems, Takehiko Yumoto was appointed as the special education officer to educate him within the Tōgū Palace.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Taish%C5%8D#cite_note-6) For these health reasons, he spent much of his youth at the Imperial villas at Hayama and Numazu, both of which are located by the sea. Although the prince showed skill in some areas, such as horse riding, he proved to be poor in areas requiring higher-level thought._[citation needed_] He was finally withdrawn from Gakushuin before finishing the middle school course in 1894. However, he did appear to have an aptitude for languages and continued to receive extensive tutoring in French, Chinese, and history from private tutors at the Akasaka Palace;_[citation needed_] Emperor Meiji gave Prince Takehito responsibility for taking care of Prince Yoshihito, and the two princes became friends.
From 1898, largely at the insistence of Itō Hirobumi, the Prince began to attend sessions of the House of Peers of the Diet of Japan as a way of learning about the political and military concerns of the country. In the same year, he gave his first official receptions to foreign diplomats, with whom he was able to shake hands and converse graciously.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Taish%C5%8D#cite_note-7) His infatuation with western culture and tendency to sprinkle French words into his conversations was a source of irritation for Emperor Meiji.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Taish%C5%8D#cite_note-8)
In October 1898, the Prince also traveled from the Numazu Imperial Villa to Kobe, Hiroshima, and Etajima, visiting sites connected with the Imperial Japanese Navy. He made another tour in 1899 to Kyūshū, visiting government offices, schools and factories (such as Yawata Iron and Steel in Fukuoka and the Mitsubishi shipyards in Nagasaki).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Taish%C5%8D#cite_note-9)

From this point onward, the Empress and her entourage wore only Western-style clothes in public. In January 1887 Empress Haruko herself issued a memorandum on the subject, stating traditional Japanese dress was not only unsuited to modern life, but Western-style dress was closer than the kimono to the clothes worn by ancient Japanese women.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empress_Sh%C5%8Dken#cite_note-6)
In the diplomatic field, Empress Haruko hosted the wife of former United States PresidentUlysses S. Grant during his visit to Japan. She was also present for her husband's meetings with Hawaiian KingKalākaua in 1881. Later that same year, she helped host the visit of the sons of future British KingEdward VII: Princes Albert Victor and George (later George V), who presented her with a pair of pet wallabies from Australia.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empress_Sh%C5%8Dken#cite_note-7)
The Emperor and the Empress ride a horse-drawn carriage to attend the constitutional celebration on 11 February 1889.
On 26 November 1886, Empress Haruko accompanied her husband to Yokosuka, Kanagawa to observe the new Imperial Japanese Navycruisers_Naniwa_ and _Takachiho_ firing torpedoes and performing other maneuvers. From 1887, the Empress was often at the Emperor's side in official visits to army maneuvers.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empress_Sh%C5%8Dken#cite_note-8) When Emperor Meiji fell ill in 1888, Empress Haruko took his place in welcoming envoys from Siam, launching warships, and visiting Tokyo Imperial University.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empress_Sh%C5%8Dken#cite_note-9) In 1889, Empress Haruko accompanied Emperor Meiji on an official visit to Nagoya and the former imperial capital of Kyoto. While he continued on to inspect naval bases at Kure and Sasebo, she visited Nara to worship at the principal Shinto shrines.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empress_Sh%C5%8Dken#cite_note-10)
texts.5:
Known throughout her tenure for supporting charity work and women's education during the First Sino-Japanese War (1894–95), Empress Haruko worked for the establishment of the Japanese Red Cross Society. She participated in the Society’s administration, especially in peacetime activities wherein she created a money fund for the International Red Cross. Renamed "The Empress Shōken Fund", it is presently used for international welfare activities. After Emperor Meiji moved his military headquarters from Tokyo to Hiroshima to be closer to the lines of communications with his troops, Empress Haruko joined him in March 1895. While in Hiroshima, she insisted on visiting hospitals full of wounded soldiers every other day of her stay.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empress_Sh%C5%8Dken#cite_note-11)
After Emperor Meiji's death in 1912, Empress Haruko was granted the title Empress Dowager (皇太后, _Kōtaigō_) by her adoptive son, Emperor Taishō. She died in 1914 at the Imperial Villa in Numazu, Shizuoka and was buried in the East Mound of the _Fushimi Momoyama Ryo_ in Fushimi, Kyoto, next to her husband. The Meiji Shrine in Tokyo was dedicated to her and her late husband.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empress_Sh%C5%8Dken#cite_note-12) On 9 May 1914, she received the posthumous name "Empress Dowager Shōken" (昭憲皇太后, _Shōken Kōtaigō_).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empress_Sh%C5%8Dken#cite_note-IHMA9th1914-1) Her railway-carriage can be seen today in the Meiji Mura Museum, in Inuyama, Aichi prefecture.
*   Grand Cordon of the Order of the Precious Crown, _1 November 1888_
She received the following orders and decorations:[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empress_Sh%C5%8Dken#cite_note-13)

steps.reasoning: We have answer: who was the mother of emperor of Japan during World War I? That emperor was Emperor Taishō (reigned 1912-1926). His mother officially was Empress Dowager Shōken (Ichijō Haruko). Note that he was also mother of by concubine Yanagiwara Naruko, but official mother was Empress Shōken. Provide answer.
steps.text:
The Emperor of Japan who reigned during World I was **Emperor Taishō** (Yoshihito Shinnō).  
His **official mother** was **Empress Dowager Shōken** (born Lady Ichijō Haruko).  

Shōken was the consort of Emperor Meiji and, after his death in 1912, was granted the title of Empress Dowager. She was considered the legal mother of her adopted son, Prince Yoshihito, who became Emperor Taishō. (His biological mother was Lady Yanagihara Naruko, a concubine of Emperor Meiji.)
